It has been proposed1 that the inconsist- ent effects on morbidity of vitamin A supplementation (see Diar- rhoea, under Deficiency States, p.1973) may be due to co-exist- ing micronutrient deficiencies, such as zinc deficiency, that affect the bioavailability of vitamin A. The authors found combined zinc and vitamin A supplementation to be more effective in re- ducing persistent diarrhoea and dysentery than either zinc or vi- tamin A alone. There is also some suggestion that zinc may po- tentiate the effects of vitamin A in the treatment of night blindness,2 but only in those patients already deficient in zinc. A study in Bangladesh3 found that the proportional improvement in vitamin A status in vitamin A-deficient children was larger in those given zinc with vitamin A than in those given vitamin A or zinc alone, suggesting a synergistic effect. Similarly, a study in Indonesia4 of supplementation in pregnant women found that betacarotene with zinc, but not betacarotene or zinc alone, im- proved vitamin A status in both mothers and infants at 6 months postpartum; the authors suggested that zinc may have a specific role in the conversion of betacarotene to retinol. 1.
